item.title: GovBrief Today #592
item.description: The Supreme Court won't let Donald Trump's post office decide who gets a mail ballot. A federal judge froze his Postal Service rule for this election, and Monday the Court refused to lift that freeze. The rule would have let the post office refuse any ballot from a voter the state had not first reported to a federal portal, and North Carolina mailed its ballots ten days ago. The states' lawsuit over whether the rule is legal at all continues in the lower courts after the election. Trump's most reliable allies, Justices Alito and Thomas, dissented. Justice Kavanaugh voted against him but wrote that the rule may well be legal, only too late for this election. I've emailed 9,091 stories over 592 straight nights, free and without ads. item.title: One of The Carol Burnett Show's most iconic and hilarious moments (from Wayback in 1976) - Made possible by the late great Bob Mackie
item.description:
From a sketch parodying Gone With the Wind... "Went with the Wind!" Carol's character (Starlett O'Hara) refashions a set of green velvet curtains into a dress to wear. The script called for the dress to be hanging off Burnett, but Mackie did not find it funny. He asked the art director for a real curtain rod and green fabric and made the dress on a mannequin. Burnett said that she came into costume fittings and when she saw the curtain rod she said it was the most brilliant sight gag ever. The laughter of the studio audience was so sustained that it had to be edited for broadcast. It was the longest-length audience reaction in the series' entire 11-year run
In 2009, Mackie and Burnett donated the dress to the National Museum of American History

item.title: South Haven, MI, Population: 3,964
item.description: SOUTH HAVEN, MI — The South Haven Police Department will begin implementing pole-based license plate readers and drone technology under a newly-approved contract. The South Haven City Council voted unanimously last Tuesday, Sept. 8, to approve a 10-year agreement with Axon Enterprise in the amount of $1,235,761. “The city has partnered with Axon since 2013, using the company’s body-worn cameras, fleet dashboard cameras, interview room recording systems, digital evidence storage system and cloud services, according to South Haven Police Chief Adam DeBoer. The new 10-year deal will cover the continued usage of each of those services, along with the addition of Axon’s drone program and 11 pole-mounted automated license plate readers that will be placed throughout the city.” “The 10-year contract allows the city to lock in equipment replacement at today’s prices, as opposed to future market value, DeBoer said. In-car dash cameras and interview room cameras get replaced every five years and body cameras every two-and-a-half years. As for the new equipment, integrating the drone software will cost the city $462,168, making up a huge portion of the new contract, DeBoer said.” “The software will allow for aerial video feeds to stream directly to officers and mobile data terminals during searches for suspects or missing individuals. “There is nothing worse than sitting a perimeter while looking for a suspect or a missing child … and not being able to see what’s going on,” he said. “It’s priceless technology.” DeBoer said the plan is to have between four and six officers become licensed through the Federal Aviation Administration, so that there is always a licensed operator working.” The 11 license plate readers, meanwhile, will monitor key thoroughfares and commercial corridors entering and exiting the city, DeBoer said. The department and Axon will work together to determine where best to place the cameras to help future investigations. “I know what the question is going to be from people in the public,” South Haven City Councilman Tom Capps said, addressing the chief. “Do we need that many license plate readers in South Haven? Do we have to have people looking after us all the time?” “While the cameras will be capturing the license plates as they go by, DeBoer said the cameras “will not be watching people,” but simply taking pictures of cars as they pass by. “When people are upset with LPRs, they say Flock,” DeBoer said. “Flock is a company that has had some downsides. We are not contracting with Flock.” Whole story: https://apple.news/AlYISGHjfQ46W7v56xS1sAA
